home.summary: The dwelling is inviolable, the Family and parents' rights are protected by the Constitution, and the State steps in only in exceptional cases, under a court's quick control.

properties.explanation: The dwelling is inviolable and may be entered by force only in accordance with law, for example by the Garda with a warrant, or without one where a child faces an immediate and serious risk.

items.text: The dwelling of every citizen is inviolable and shall not be forcibly entered save in accordance with law.

properties.explanation: The Family is protected in its constitution and authority, and the courts recognise a constitutional right to privacy among the personal rights.

items.text: The State guarantees in its laws to respect, and, as far as practicable, by its laws to defend and vindicate the personal rights of the citizen.

text: 1° The State recognises the Family as the natural primary and fundamental unit group of Society, and as a moral institution possessing inalienable and imprescriptible rights, antecedent and superior to all positive law.
2° The State, therefore, guarantees to protect the Family in its constitution and authority, as the necessary basis of social order and as indispensable to the welfare of the Nation and the State.

properties.explanation: Private ownership is a natural right that no law may abolish; its exercise may be regulated by law for the common good.

items.text: The State shall, in particular, by its laws protect as best it may from unjust attack and, in the case of injustice done, vindicate the life, person, good name, and property rights of every citizen.

text: 1 1° The State acknowledges that man, in virtue of his rational being, has the natural right, antecedent to positive law, to the private ownership of external goods.
2° The State accordingly guarantees to pass no law attempting to abolish the right of private ownership or the general right to transfer, bequeath, and inherit property.
2 1° The State recognises, however, that the exercise of the rights mentioned in the foregoing provisions of this Article ought, in civil society, to be regulated by the principles of social justice.
2° The State, accordingly, may as occasion requires delimit by law the exercise of the said rights with a view to reconciling their exercise with the exigencies of the common good.

properties.explanation: Parents are the primary educators and carers, and the State steps in only in exceptional cases, by proportionate means. A child can be taken without a court order only when there is an immediate and serious risk, and then the Agency must bring the case to a judge within three days; an emergency care order lasts at most eight days, and longer care needs a court's finding of actual or likely harm.

items.text: The State acknowledges that the primary and natural educator of the child is the Family and guarantees to respect the inalienable right and duty of parents to provide, according to their means, for the religious and moral, intellectual, physical and social education of their children.

In exceptional cases, where the parents, regardless of their marital status, fail in their duty towards their children to such extent that the safety or welfare of any of their children is likely to be prejudicially affected, the State as guardian of the common good shall, by proportionate means as provided by law, endeavour to supply the place of the parents, but always with due regard for the natural and imprescriptible rights of the child.

Where a member of the Garda Síochána has reasonable grounds for believing that— (a) there is an immediate and serious risk to the health or welfare of a child, and (b) it would not be sufficient for the protection of the child from such immediate and serious risk to await the making of an application for an emergency care order by the Child and Family Agency under section 13, or an application for a warrant under section 35, the member, accompanied by such other persons as may be necessary, may, without warrant, enter (if need be by force) any house or other place … and remove the child to safety.

Where a child is delivered up to the custody of the Child and Family Agency in accordance with subsection (3), the Agency shall, unless it returns the child to the parent having custody of him or a person acting in loco parentis or an order referred to in section 35 has been made in respect of the child, make application for an emergency care order at the next sitting of the District Court held in the same district court district or, in the event that the next such sitting is not due to be held within three days of the date on which the child is delivered up to the custody of the Agency, at a sitting of the District Court, which has been specially arranged under section 13(4), held within the said three days, and it shall be lawful for the Agency to retain custody of the child pending the hearing of that application.
An emergency care order shall place the child under the care of the Child and Family Agency for a period of eight days or such shorter period as may be specified in the order.

properties.explanation: Married parents are joint guardians of their child, and so is an unmarried father who has lived with the mother for 12 consecutive months, including 3 after the birth; other fathers become guardians by agreement or court order. A guardian can ask a court to settle a question only when they disagree.

items.text: The following persons shall be guardians of a child jointly: (a) the father and mother of the child, or (b) where a married couple of the same sex have jointly adopted a child under an adoption order, each of the married couple.
Any person being a guardian of a child may apply to the court for its direction on any question affecting the welfare of the child and the court may make such order as it thinks proper.

properties.explanation: The Constitution protects children's own rights, and a court may place a child in care only where it finds the child has been, or is likely to be, harmed or neglected and will not otherwise get the care they need.

items.text: The State recognises and affirms the natural and imprescriptible rights of all children and shall, as far as practicable, by its laws protect and vindicate those rights.

Where, on the application of the Child and Family Agency with respect to a child, the court is satisfied that— (a) the child has been or is being assaulted, ill-treated, neglected or sexually abused, or (b) the child's health, development or welfare has been or is being avoidably impaired or neglected, or (c) the child's health, development or welfare is likely to be avoidably impaired or neglected, and that the child requires care or protection which he is unlikely to receive unless the court makes an order under this section, the court may make an order (in this Act referred to as a "care order") in respect of the child.

properties.explanation: Victims can get a safety order or a barring order that removes the abuser from the home, and an interim barring order at once where there is an immediate risk of significant harm.

Where the court, on application to it for a barring order or between the making of that application and its determination, is of the opinion … that there are reasonable grounds for believing— (a) there is an immediate risk of significant harm to the applicant or a dependent person, and (b) the making of a protection order would not be sufficient to protect the applicant or a dependent person, the court shall … by order (in this Act referred to as an "interim barring order")— (i) direct the respondent, if residing at a place where the applicant or the dependent person resides, to leave the place, …

properties.explanation: Parents have a constitutional right to educate their children at home. But they must apply to the Child and Family Agency to register the child, which assesses whether the child receives a 'certain minimum education' and can refuse registration.

items.text: Parents shall be free to provide this education in their homes or in private schools or in schools recognised or established by the State.

text: 1° The State shall not oblige parents in violation of their conscience and lawful preference to send their children to schools established by the State, or to any particular type of school designated by the State.
2° The State shall, however, as guardian of the common good, require in view of actual conditions that the children receive a certain minimum education, moral, intellectual and social.

items.text: … where a parent chooses to educate, or have educated, his or her child in a place other than a recognised school he or she shall, in accordance with this section, apply to the Child and Family Agency to have the child concerned registered in the register.
items.fix: … where a parent chooses to educate, or have educated, his or her child in a place other than a recognised school he or she shall notify the Child and Family Agency, which shall enter the child in the register.
items.why: Home education becomes a notification, not an application the Agency can refuse.

items.text: … the Child and Family Agency shall— (a) if satisfied that the child concerned is receiving a certain minimum education, register the child concerned in the register, or (b) if not so satisfied— (i) register the child … subject to the parent … undertaking to comply with such requirements …, or (ii) refuse to register the child concerned …
items.fix: Where the Child and Family Agency has reasonable grounds to believe that a child registered under this section is not receiving a certain minimum education, it may apply to the District Court, which may, after hearing the parents and the child, require the child to attend a recognised school.
items.why: Only a court, on evidence, can override the parents' choice, as with other limits on parental rights (Constitution Art. 42A.2).

fix: (1) A local referendum in the area of a local authority, or of a municipal district, local electoral area, town, village or neighbourhood within it, may be proposed by an initiative committee supported by the signatures of not less than one hundredth of the local government electors registered there.

(2) The elected council shall hold the referendum where the proposal is supported by the signatures of not less than one fiftieth of those electors, collected within six months, and may decide to hold it on a proposal supported by fewer.

(3) A referendum may be held on any matter within the functions of the local authority, including its budget and the local adjustment factor of the local property tax, and voters may decide on a draft resolution, bye-law or plan, which, if approved, takes effect as worded.
(4) The proposal shall be held to be approved if a majority of the votes cast are in its favour, regardless of turnout.
(5) A petition shall not lapse because the term of the elected council ends; the newly elected council shall decide on it within one month of its first meeting.
items.why: Lets residents propose a local referendum with 1/100 of electors and oblige the council to hold it with 1/50, on any local matter, decided by the majority of those who vote. The same thresholds as proposed for Bulgaria.

properties.explanation: Irish law provides no meeting of the residents of a neighbourhood that takes binding decisions; councils may only consult the public.

items.text: In this section "transferable vote" means a vote which is— (a) capable of being given so as to indicate the voter's preference for the candidates in order, and (b) capable of being transferred to the next choice when the vote is not required to give a prior choice the necessary quota of votes, or when, owing to the deficiency in the number of the votes given for a prior choice, that choice is excluded from the list of candidates.

properties.explanation: Each council has a number of members fixed by law (Fingal, for example, has 40). With the single transferable vote, candidates tend to focus on their own part of the area, so each councillor answers to particular voters.
